paper.title: Chunked Budget Allocation Prevents Non-Monotonic Regressions in World-Model Verification
paper.abstract: World models that predict environment dynamics can serve as pre-execution verifiers for agents facing irreversible actions. However, sequential verify-and-retry---where rejected actions trigger agent re-planning---can paradoxically \emph{reduce} task success as verification budget increases. We identify \emph{trajectory drift} as the root cause: when verification rejects a checkout (often a false negative), the agent re-browses and frequently selects a worse product than originally found. We propose \emph{chunked budget allocation}: instead of spreading verification budget across many sequential cycles, spend it in fewer cycles with more parallel rollouts per cycle. On WebShop, chunked verification ($M=1$ cycle) achieves 21.50\% task success versus 0.86\% for sequential verify-and-retry ($M=10$ cycles)---a 25$\times$ improvement at the same budget. Surprisingly, consensus aggregation across parallel rollouts provides no benefit over single-rollout acceptance, as the world model's poor calibration (predicting failure for 98.4\% of cycles) causes consensus to degenerate. Our results demonstrate that budget allocation structure matters more than aggregation sophistication when world models are poorly calibrated.

content.summary: This paper studies a verification-based agent where a text-based world model is utilized to justify whether the agent needs to recycle. They claim that the commonly used sequential verify-and-retry protocol can induce trajectory drift and reduce the performance. The proposed solution is simple: allocate a fixed verification budget in larger parallel chunks and fewer sequential cycles. On WebShop, the paper reports a large improvement over sequential verification at the same budget, and further argues that the gain comes from reducing sequential cycles.
content.strengths: This paper provides a case study on a verification-based agent loop and identifies a failure mode that might provide insights for future study.
content.weaknesses:
1. The main concern is that this paper is mainly talking about how to reduce damage from a poor verifier, and current results do not even provide a comparison with a no-verification agent. I'm really wondering whether it's a meaningful topic.
2. The novelty is limited, as mentioned before, this paper just gives a case study.
3. The failure analysis is not fully convincing. The paper reports that trajectory drift accounts for 60.5% where chunked succeeds and sequential fails, but the labeling procedure is not described clearly. It is also a selected subset of episodes, not a global decomposition over all failures.
